specAnchors.text: understand the mechanisms of the nucleophilic substitution reactions between primary halogenoalkanes and: i aqueous potassium hydroxide ii ammonia S N 1 and S N 2 substitution mechanisms will be tested in Unit 4.
be able to deduce a reaction mechanism, using knowledge of the rate equation and the stoichiometric equation for a reaction

primer.text: Kinetic evidence can only suggest a mechanism, never prove one, though it can disprove a wrong one. This note checks elementary steps against the overall equation, deduces orders from a known rate-determining step, and contrasts the SN1 route of tertiary halogenoalkanes with the SN2 route of primary ones, whose one-step rate law names both reactants.

modules.title: What kinetics can and cannot prove
sourceHeadings: Predicting the reaction order & deducing the rate equation
modules.opening: Kinetic evidence can only suggest a mechanism, never prove it, though one wrong order can kill a proposal outright. Elementary steps must add back to the overall equation, and when the slow step is known, orders fall out of it directly: the NO-plus-hydrogen mechanism shows a slow step built from one N2O2 and one H2, giving rate = k[NO]^2[H2].
keyPoints: Kinetics can only suggest a mechanism, but it can disprove a proposed one.
Elementary steps are the individual stages of a mechanism, and they must combine to the overall stoichiometric equation.
For 2NO plus 2H2 forming N2 and 2H2O, the slow second step uses one N2O2 and one H2.
Because N2O2 forms from two NO molecules, the reaction is second order in NO and first order in H2, giving rate = k[NO]^2[H2] and third order overall.
Intermediates such as N2O2 cannot appear in the rate equation, which is why the substitution through two NO molecules is needed.

low.restatement: Match the slow step's contents to orders: N2O2 (from 2 NO) plus H2 gives rate = k[NO]^2[H2]; intermediates never appear in rate equations.
low.analogy: A receipt lists finished goods, not the factory's half-made parts: the rate equation names added species, never intermediates.
low.examPointer: Check any proposed mechanism by adding its steps - if the sum misses the overall equation, the proposal is dead.

medium.restatement: The slow step is where the rate lives, so its ingredient list is the rate equation's draft; an intermediate on that list must be replaced by the species that make it.
medium.analogy: A recipe that calls for a sauce already in the fridge: to shop, you list the sauce's own ingredients instead of the sauce.
medium.examPointer: The substitution step (intermediate replaced by its precursors) is the mark-scoring move in these questions.

modules.title: The SN1 route of tertiary halogenoalkanes
modules.opening: Tertiary halogenoalkanes substitute by an SN1 path: the carbon-halogen bond breaks first and alone, making a carbocation, and the nucleophile attacks afterwards. One species in the slow step means one term in the rate equation, hence the name's '1'.
keyPoints: In tertiary halogenoalkanes the halogen-bearing carbon is bonded to three alkyl groups.
SN1 stands for substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular: the slow step depends on one reagent only, the halogenoalkane.
The SN1 mechanism is two-step: the C-X bond breaks heterolytically first (slow, rate-determining), releasing X- and a carbocation.
The nucleophile then attacks the carbocation in a fast second step.

low.restatement: SN1: bond breaks first (slow) making a carbocation, nucleophile attacks second (fast); rate = k[halogenoalkane].
low.analogy: A lock that springs open on its own before anyone inserts a key: the springing (ionisation) is the slow act, and the key (nucleophile) enters afterwards.
low.examPointer: The '1' counts species in the slow step - quote that when explaining the label.

medium.restatement: Carbocation stability is what makes the wait worthwhile: three alkyl groups steady the positive centre, so tertiary substrates can afford a two-step route.
medium.analogy: A celebrity leaving a venue: the hard part is stepping out alone into the crowd (ionisation); the escort (nucleophile) arrives once the exit exists.
medium.examPointer: Tertiary-only behaviour is the SN1 exam signature.

modules.title: The SN2 route of primary halogenoalkanes
modules.opening: Primary halogenoalkanes cannot wait for a cation, so the nucleophile attacks as the halide leaves - one concerted step. Two species share the slow step, the rate equation names both, and bromoethane with hydroxide shows the backside attack that inverts the carbon's geometry.
keyPoints: In primary halogenoalkanes the halogen-bearing carbon is bonded to one alkyl group.
SN2 means substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular: the rate depends on both the halogenoalkane and the nucleophile.
The SN2 mechanism is one step: the nucleophile donates a lone pair to the delta-positive carbon while the C-X bond breaks, the halogen leaving as X-.
The rate equation for SN2 is rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile], and the step is bimolecular.
Bromoethane with hydroxide giving ethanol shows the mechanism, with attack from the far side causing inversion of configuration.

low.restatement: SN2: one concerted step, nucleophile attacking while X- leaves; rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile]; backside attack inverts the centre.
low.analogy: A revolving door pushed from behind as the passenger steps out: entry and exit are one motion, and both pusher and passenger count.
low.examPointer: The '2' counts two species in the slow step; the inversion detail is the diagram mark.

medium.restatement: With no alkyl shielding, the primary carbon is approachable, so bond-making and bond-breaking fuse into a single event whose rate needs both partners.
medium.analogy: Two people passing a sofa through a doorway: both must act together, and neither alone moves the sofa.
medium.examPointer: Primary-only behaviour is the SN2 exam signature; secondary can go either way.

glossary.definition: One stage of a proposed mechanism; the steps must sum to the overall equation.
Two-step substitution through a carbocation, with rate = k[halogenoalkane].
One-step concerted substitution, with rate = k[halogenoalkane][nucleophile].
The positive carbon centre formed when the C-X bond breaks in an SN1 route.
